thread.title: Intel’s Chip Lead Disappearing, Says Linley Group

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Intel’s Chip Lead Disappearing, Says Linley Group

organizations.name: says linley group by tiernan ray updated

text:
By Tiernan Ray Updated April 16, 2018 6:52 p.m. ET Intel's bunny suit technicians are losing the lead in chip manufacturing the company long maintained over rivals such as Taiwan Semi. Illustration: Intel Inc. Intel ’s( INTC ) long-held lead in making the best integrated circuits in the world is “disappearing,” according to a report today in the chip-industry newsletter Microprocessor Report .
Lead analyst Linley Gwennap , head of the eponymous Linley Group research firm, writes that after repeated delays by Intel with its “10-nanometer process,” its attempts to manufacture chips with dimensions as small as 10 billionths of an inch, the company is falling behind competitors Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM ), the world’s large contract chip maker, and Samsung Electronics ( 005930KS ), and Samsung’s partner, privately held GlobalFoundries .
The three challengers produce chips for Intel competitors such as Qualcomm ( QCOM ), and for large customers such as Apple ( AAPL ), so it’s not just a technology battle, it's a risk to Intel’s chip sales.
Gwennap’s article goes into extensive detail about the “ density ” of the chip circuitry each party produces, and other metrics by which to compare them, and comes up with very careful comparisons of the various’ companies’ offerings.
His conclusion is that while there are differences of nomenclature between the various technologies, it’s not just about semantics, the competitors are really closing the gap with Intel.
No matter what you call these various technologies, Gwennap writes that the “7-nanometer” technology of TSM and Samsung and Global should be quite close to Intel’s 10-nanometer process, with the result that "the three leading foundries, which serve all of Intel’s major competitors, [will be] on the same level as the x86 giant."
Taiwan Semi’s 7-nano technology “appears similar to Intel’s 10nm, within a fraction of a node,” he writes. It’s even possible the three competitors will leap-frog Intel’s results before the chip giant can move to its next technology, sometime in 2021, writes Gwennap.
One interesting risk for the challengers: They’ll be moving faster than Intel to the next form of chip-making lithography , from equipment maker ASML ( ASML ). As noted recently , and as Gwennap acknowledges, that technology brings its own risks in the manufacturing process.
Intel shares today were up 54 cents, or 1%, at $52.40.
